source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Askgaard_2015_DrinkingPatternCirrhosisCohort.pdf, pp. 1–7 of the online-first PDF (Journal of Hepatology, article in press; all pages read); Tables 1–4 and Figures 1–2 checked on rendered pages 2–5. Supplementary material (Supplementary Tables 2A–6A, 5 and 6) not read.

claims.overstatement: None. The paper's own 'no risk of alcoholic cirrhosis among lifetime abstainers' (zero cases among 63 men and 265 women, for an outcome defined as alcoholic) is not carried into the claim.
claims.note: Every Askgaard number in the statement and magnitude matches p. 2, p. 3 and Fig. 1 (checked on the rendered pages), and the editors' conversions are right (257/26,696 = 0.96%, about 1 in 100; 85/29,221 = 0.29%, about 3 in 1,000). The hazard ratios' reference is named correctly in the claim ('against fewer than 14'). But the opening frame 'compared with not drinking (lifetime or long-term abstainers)' does not fit this cohort, whose reference is people drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week (lifetime abstainers had no cases and are not in the model). Suggest 'against people who drank fewer than 14 drinks (12 g each) a week'. Whether this cohort is one of the 2019 review's studies cannot be checked from this source. Reporting issue: the listed exclusions (86 + 105 + 27 + 27 + 50 + 236 + 7 = 538) do not account for the drop from 57,053 participants to 55,917 analysed; 598 are unexplained.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Study population, 1st paragraph; Follow-up, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort: 160,725 people aged 50–64 invited December 1993 to May 1997, 27,178 men and 29,875 women took part (35%); 55,917 analysed (26,696 men, 29,221 women; Table 1). Outcome: register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis (National Patient Register, Register of Causes of Death; ICD-8 571.0, ICD-10 K70.3); follow-up to 31 December 2011, 831,285 person-years, median 14.9 years (14.6 men, 15.1 women). 257 men and 85 women diagnosed, 66 and 19 per 100,000 person-years (recomputed from Table 4 person-years: 257/389,112 and 85/442,173, same).

No cases among lifetime abstainers. Against people drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week (Fig. 1 category 0–14; current abstainers shown separately): 14–28 drinks a week HR 2.33 (1.52–3.58) in men, 3.49 (2.00–6.12) in women; 28–42 drinks 6.98 (4.65–10.5) and 16.2 (9.16–28.7); higher categories (men 42–56, 56–70, >70; women >42 pooled) only in Fig. 1, rising further. Current abstainers 7.58 (3.39–16.9) in men, 3.21 (0.77–13.4) in women. Adjusted for smoking, education and waist circumference (Fig. 1 legend), age as time scale (p. 2).

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Information on alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph; Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Weekly amounts of beer (330-ml bottles), wine (125-ml glasses) and spirits (30-ml drinks) reported once, at baseline, and converted to standard drinks of 12 g ethanol; amounts at ages 20–29, 30–39, 40–49 and 50–59 recalled at baseline. Lifetime abstainers and current abstainers (former drinkers) kept as separate categories, so the reference group is people who drank little, not abstainers.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Only 35% of those invited took part and they may live more healthily; women's incidence somewhat lower than national data predict; alcohol self-reported, women possibly under-reporting more than men; few cases in women; deaths only 11% of cases, too few to separate mortality from morbidity; no hepatitis C data (low prevalence in Denmark).

claims.overstatement: None in the claim, which says 'is associated with' where the source says daily drinking 'increases' risk (pp. 6–7). Flag for the editor: the sentence relaying the authors' advice that people who drink daily drink less often is advice on drinking frequency (no amount); it is attributed and qualified, but the editor may decide whether it belongs in a claim.
claims.note: Every Askgaard number in the statement and magnitude matches Tables 1–3 and pp. 2–4 (checked on the rendered pages). The four editors' calculations recompute to the same rounded figures: 171/7276 = 2.35 in 100, 27/9165 = 2.9 in 1,000, 30/3931 = 7.6 in 1,000, 15/9481 = 1.6 in 1,000. 'Not in the cohort paper's main text' is right for 2.25 (1.68–3.00) and 1.28 (0.82–2.02): I searched the text, and they can only come from the supplement. 'No funding stated, no conflicts declared' matches p. 7. Could add: participation was 35%; amount entered the frequency models as a continuous term while risk rises steeply with amount (Fig. 1), so some confounding by amount may remain beyond what the authors say (editors' consideration). The text–table mismatch for women drinking one day a week (anchor 5) does not touch the claim.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Study population, Information on alcohol consumption and Follow-up, 1st paragraphs
anchors.extracted: 55,917 adults aged 50–64 enrolled December 1993 to May 1997 (35% of 160,725 invited); frequency asked once at baseline (never, <1 day a month, 1–3 days a month, once a week, 2–4 days, 5–6 days, daily); amount in 12-g standard drinks a week; outcome a register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis (ICD-8 571.0, ICD-10 K70.3); median follow-up 14.9 years.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Statistical analysis, 1st, 4th and 6th paragraphs; Introduction, last paragraph
anchors.extracted: Cox models with age as time axis, adjusted for smoking (4 levels), education (≤7, 8–10, ≥11 years) and waist (WHO cut-offs); proportional hazards checked. Frequency analysed three ways: amount as a continuous term with a trend test among drinkers; amount linear within frequency groups with a test of equal slopes; amount in categories with a likelihood-ratio interaction test. All analyses by sex. Only average amount and frequency known, so binge drinking could not be studied.

Men: 9165 drank on 2–4 days a week (median 8.9, 5th–95th percentile 3.6–13, drinks a week), 4495 on 5–6 days (19, 7.0–42), 7276 daily (26, 9.4–60); smokers 34% vs 47%. Women: 9481 on 2–4 days (6.6, 3.0–19), 3147 on 5–6 days (13, 5.9–27), 3931 daily (19, 7.3–40); smokers 27% vs 43%. Spearman correlation of frequency with amount 0.77 (men), 0.85 (women).

anchors.locator: Table 2, men; Results › Alcohol drinking frequency, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Men, against 2–4 days a week: 27 cases (135,573 person-years) at 2–4 days, 30 (66,512) at 5–6 days, 171 (103,820) daily. Daily HR 8.29 (5.52–12.4) for age, 4.83 (3.20–7.29) adding amount, 3.65 (2.39–5.55) adding smoking, education and waist; 5–6 days 2.26 (1.35–3.81), 1.69 (1.00–2.85), 1.43 (0.84–2.43); current abstainers 10.0 (4.32–23.0); trend P < 0.001 in all three models (abstainers excluded). Amount adjustment changed the estimates most (p. 3). Crude 171/7276 = 2.35% and 27/9165 = 0.29% (editors' calculation).

anchors.locator: Table 2, women; Results › Alcohol drinking frequency, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Women, against 2–4 days a week: 15 cases (144,603 person-years) at 2–4 days, 17 (47,775) at 5–6 days, 30 (58,414) daily. Daily 5.01 (2.69–9.31) for age, 1.6 (0.81–3.30) adding amount, 1.73 (0.85–3.52) fully adjusted; 5–6 days 3.44 (1.72–6.88), 2.07 (1.02–4.18), 2.30 (1.14–4.67); less than weekly 1.45 (0.71–2.96); trend P < 0.001, 0.57, 0.14. Crude 30/3931 = 0.76% and 15/9481 = 0.16% (editors' calculation). The text's fully adjusted one-day-a-week HR, 0.73 (0.27–2.01), is the table's age-adjusted value; the table's fully adjusted value is 0.81 (0.29–2.24).

anchors.locator: Table 3; Results › Alcohol drinking frequency, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Adjusted HR per extra weekly drink by frequency: men 1.02 (1.01–1.03) at <1 day a week, 1.03 (1.02–1.05) at 1–4 days, 1.03 (1.02–1.03) at 5–6 days, 1.05 (1.04–1.05) daily; women 1.09 (1.05–1.13), 1.06 (1.03–1.10), 1.08 (1.06–1.09), 1.05 (1.04–1.06). Frequency interaction significant in men (P < 0.0001) and women (P = 0.0007): steepest slope among men who drank daily, among women in those who drank least often.

HRs by amount category and frequency are only in Supplementary Table 5 (not read). Within each amount category, people who drank daily drank somewhat more on average, which the authors say makes frequency and amount hard to disentangle. The 2019 review's figures for this cohort (2.25, 1.68–3.00; 1.28, 0.82–2.02) do not appear anywhere in the main text.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Comparison with other studies, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs; Conclusions (pp. 6–7)
anchors.extracted: Authors: in men daily drinking carried a higher risk with amount taken into account; in women no firm conclusions for low power. They read the men's result as confirming that daily drinking increases risk; the raised risk in women drinking less than weekly may include people with drinking problems, and the women's 5–6-day excess over daily drinking may be information bias; they propose advising people who drink daily to drink less often and conclude daily drinking appears to raise risk regardless of amount, at least in men. No change in drinking was observed.

35% participation, participants possibly healthier than non-participants; self-reported alcohol, women possibly under-reporting; low number of cases in women makes conclusions on drinking pattern in women difficult.
The authors declare nothing to disclose regarding funding or conflicts of interest; no funding source is named.

claims.note: All four HRs and the incidence figures match p. 3, Fig. 1 and p. 2; the medians 19 against 26 match Table 1. 'No source tested the sex difference' holds here (sex-stratified analyses only, p. 2), and the intervals overlap at both amount levels. The authors' 'too few for firm conclusions' is said of women's results in general and of drinking pattern in particular; the claim's paraphrase is fair. Could add: the per-drink HRs (1.05 in women against 1.03 in men, anchor 2) point the same way; and the authors note that women may under-report drinking more than men (anchor 4), so part of the sex difference in relative risk per reported drink could be an artefact (editors' inference).

anchors.extracted: Against people of the same sex drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week (analyses stratified by sex, p. 2): 14–28 drinks a week 3.49 (2.00–6.12) in women and 2.33 (1.52–3.58) in men; 28–42 drinks 16.2 (9.16–28.7) and 6.98 (4.65–10.5); intervals overlap at both levels; women above 42 drinks grouped because few. No test of a sex difference.

anchors.locator: Results › Lifetime alcohol amount, 2nd paragraph; Table 4
anchors.extracted: HR per extra weekly drink at baseline, adjusted for age, smoking, education and waist: 1.05 (1.04–1.06) in women against 1.03 (1.03–1.04) in men; per drink over lifetime 1.05 (1.04–1.07) against 1.04 (1.04–1.05). Not in the claim.
Incidence 19 per 100,000 person-years in women and 66 in men; women drank less at each frequency (median drinks a week: daily 19 vs 26; 5–6 days 13 vs 19; 2–4 days 6.6 vs 8.9).

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Authors: among women no firm conclusions for low statistical power; the low number of cases among women (85) makes conclusions on drinking pattern difficult; women's incidence lower than national figures predict; some studies suggest women under-report drinking more than men.
Stated as background: women have a higher risk of alcoholic cirrhosis than men at a given intake, citing Rehm et al. (2010) and a 2004 Danish study; second-hand.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in my blind reading: 538 listed exclusions against a gap of 1136; 598 unexplained.
Found independently in my blind reading.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E, high overall, driven by confounding by amount for the frequency results and by single baseline and recalled exposure. As the card says, the amount gradient alone would merit a milder judgment.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: causal and advisory language on frequency although frequency and amount could not be separated; women's frequency pattern unlike men's; 'no risk' among lifetime abstainers for an outcome defined by drinking.

missed: In the main frequency models (Table 2), amount entered as a continuous term (Materials and methods › Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph, p. 2 of the online-first PDF). Because risk rises steeply across amount categories (Fig. 1), a linear adjustment may leave confounding by amount in the daily-drinking HRs; this supports the card's confounding judgment but is not stated on the card.
